content.overview: Bailment is delivery of goods for a purpose with a condition of return or directed disposal (s. 148). Pledge is bailment as security for a debt or promise (s. 172).

sections.heading: Bailment duties
sections.body: Bailee must take care as a man of ordinary prudence would of his own goods (s. 151) and avoid unauthorised use.

sections.heading: Pledge
sections.body: Pawnee may retain and, on default, sell after notice (s. 176), accounting for surplus.

sections.heading: Track B
sections.body: Plead delivery, purpose, and breach of care or wrongful sale. Document notice before pledge sale.

illustrations: A lends a horse to B knowing it is vicious but does not disclose the danger; the horse injures B. Section 150’s statutory illustration makes the bailor responsible for the resulting damage.

Statutory rule: Sections 148–171 regulate bailment, including delivery, disclosure of faults, the bailee’s standard of care, return and liabilities, liens and the finder’s rights; sections 172–179 regulate pledge and the pawnee’s statutory rights on default.

Definition: Bailment is delivery of goods by one person to another for a purpose on the condition that the goods will be returned or otherwise dealt with according to the bailor’s directions; pledge is bailment of goods as security for a debt or performance.

Ingredients / conditions:
1. Identify the goods and the bailor/bailee or pawnor/pawnee relationship.
2. For bailment, prove delivery or possession for a defined purpose and the agreed return/disposition.
3. Apply the statutory duties of disclosure, care, return and authorised use.
4. For pledge, identify the secured obligation and apply the pawnee’s retention, expense and default-sale rights subject to the Act.

distinctions: Bailment vs pledge: pledge is a species of bailment in which possession is delivered as security for a debt or performance.
Bailment vs sale: bailment ordinarily transfers possession for a purpose without transferring ownership, whereas a sale transfers ownership.
